opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really one of the core design questions we had to grapple with, because there's no such thing as a single "energy score" for AI that makes sense across the board. Generating an image is fundamentally different from classifying a sentence, and if you just put all models on one list, you'd basically be comparing apples and, I don't know, freight trains.

So the approach I think makes the most sense is to evaluate models within a task. You define a set of concrete tasks: text classification, question answering, summarization, text generation, image classification, image generation, speech recognition, and so on. For each one, you pick a standardized dataset and a fixed number of queries, run every model under the same hardware and the same conditions, and measure the energy consumed for that workload. Then you compare models only against others doing the same thing. That gives you something meaningful, like: for summarization, this model uses this much energy per thousand queries, and this other one uses ten times more.

Within each task, a relative rating is really helpful, something like a star system or a letter grade, the way appliances have energy labels. Most people don't have an intuition for what a watt-hour per query means, but they do understand "this one is five stars and that one is one star." That relative framing is also more robust over time, because as models get more efficient you can rescale the ratings.

Modality matters a lot, too. What we've seen consistently is that generative tasks are far more energy-intensive than discriminative ones, and image generation in particular sits at the very top, often orders of magnitude more than text classification. Multi-purpose generative models used for tasks a small, specialized model could handle are also much more expensive. So part of the point of separating by task is to make that visible. If you just need sentiment analysis, you don't need a giant general-purpose model, and the leaderboard should help people see the cost of that choice.

There are also nuances you have to be transparent about. Output length matters a lot for generation, so you have to control or at least report it. Hardware, batching, precision, and quantization all change the numbers, so you either fix them or document them clearly. And ideally you're measuring inference specifically, since that's where most of the energy goes once a model is deployed at scale, though training costs matter too.

And finally, I'd love to see this go beyond open models. Right now the biggest gap is that a lot of the most widely used systems are closed, so we just don't know their energy use. A good leaderboard framework should have a way for companies to submit and verify their own numbers under the same protocol. Otherwise we're only ever measuring part of the picture, and probably not the most energy-hungry part.

r001.rationale: The response says image generation can use orders of magnitude more energy than text classification. It does not make that claim about image-involving AI tasks generally.

r002.rationale: The response recommends comparing models performing the same task, but does not specifically recommend comparing multimodal models with other multimodal models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a lot, because the first instinct people have is, "let's just rank all the models by energy use," and that's actually really misleading. A model that generates images and a model that classifies text are not doing the same thing, so putting them on the same leaderboard is like comparing the fuel efficiency of a truck and a bicycle. It doesn't tell you anything useful.

So the way we approached it with the AI Energy Score project was to define a fixed set of tasks, things like text generation, summarization, image classification, image generation, speech-to-text, and so on, and then for each task we have a standardized dataset and a standardized number of queries. Every model gets run on the same hardware, with the same batch size, the same settings, and we measure the energy consumed per, say, a thousand queries. And then the ranking is within the task. So you're comparing text generation models to other text generation models, image generation models to other image generation models. That's the only comparison that actually makes sense.

The other piece is the scoring itself. We went with a star rating, kind of like the Energy Star labels you see on appliances, where five stars is the most efficient and one star is the least. And those thresholds are relative to the distribution of models within that task. So a five-star image generation model is still going to use orders of magnitude more energy than a one-star text classification model, and that's fine, because the point isn't to tell people "don't generate images." The point is, if you've already decided you need to generate images, here's how to pick the model that does it with the least energy.

Where it gets tricky is modalities that are kind of hybrid, or tasks where output length varies a lot. With text generation, for instance, a model that writes a two-sentence answer and one that writes three paragraphs are going to look very different, and that's not entirely an efficiency question, it's a behavior question. So we try to control for that as much as we can, but you have to be honest that there's some noise. And then there's the whole question of reasoning models that generate a lot of hidden tokens before they answer. That's energy you're paying for that the user never sees, and we think it absolutely should count, because it's real electricity.

I'd also say the leaderboard shouldn't be static. The tasks people actually use these models for shift over time, so the categories need to evolve, and we've been trying to get the community to contribute, both in terms of submitting models and in terms of proposing new task definitions. Because ultimately what I want is for this to be something a developer looks at before they deploy, the same way you'd look at latency or cost, and for that it has to reflect the things they're actually building.

r001.rationale: The response says even a five-star image-generation model uses orders of magnitude more energy than a one-star text-classification model, clearly conveying the image-versus-text energy gap.

r002.rationale: It recommends comparing models within the same task, such as image-generation models with other image-generation models. It does not specifically recommend comparing multimodal models with other multimodal models.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to compare systems within tasks, because there isn’t one meaningful efficiency number that covers everything. Generating an image and classifying a sentence are doing very different things. Even within text generation, the length of the input and the output matters, so you have to make those conditions explicit.

And you need to put energy consumption alongside performance. If a model uses less energy but doesn’t do the task well enough, that’s not necessarily a useful improvement. I’d like to see leaderboards where you can look at a particular task, choose the level of performance you need, and see what the energy cost is across models.

The measurement setup matters, too: the hardware, the batch size, what you’re actually including in the measurement. Otherwise, you could be ranking differences in infrastructure rather than differences in models. So I’d favor a set of task-specific comparisons with a common, transparent measurement methodology, rather than a single overall winner.

r001.rationale: It says image generation and sentence classification differ, but gives no claim that image tasks use orders of magnitude more energy.

r002.rationale: It recommends comparing systems within tasks, but does not specifically recommend comparing multimodal models with other multimodal models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to compare like with like. A model that generates an image is doing something very different from a model that classifies text, so putting them on one leaderboard with a single efficiency score isn’t necessarily meaningful.

I’d organize it by task and modality, and then show energy use alongside performance. For a given level of accuracy or quality, how much energy does it take to do the task? And we need consistent measurement conditions, because the hardware, batch size, and length of the inputs and outputs can all affect that comparison.

The goal is to help people choose an appropriate model for what they actually need. If your application is sentiment analysis, you should be able to compare models on sentiment analysis, rather than assume that a large, general-purpose generative model is the best tool for the job.

r001.rationale: The response says image generation and text classification are different tasks, but does not state that image tasks use orders of magnitude more energy.
